failures.title: BMW S65B40 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Rod bearing wear - the S65's biggest weakness
items.whatHappens: The factory rod bearings have excessively tight clearances, leading to premature wear and, in severe cases, catastrophic engine failure. The original tin‑aluminium bearings are prone to starving of oil at high RPM, particularly when the engine is cold or during sustained high‑G cornering. Symptoms include metallic shavings in the oil, a knocking sound from the bottom end, and eventual bearing spin - which typically writes off the crankshaft and often the entire engine.
items.repairVsReplace: Preventative rod bearing replacement (around £1,500-£2,500 at an M specialist) is strongly recommended at 60,000 miles and is far cheaper than a full engine replacement. If the bearings have already failed and damaged the crank, a full rebuild or replacement is almost always required. Read our full rod bearing failure guide

items.title: Throttle actuator failure
items.whatHappens: The S65 uses individual throttle bodies actuated by electric motors. The internal gears in the throttle actuators wear over time, causing drivetrain malfunctions, reduced power and, in some cases, complete throttle failure. This is a well‑documented issue across the S65 platform.
items.repairVsReplace: The actuators can be rebuilt (gear replacement) or replaced entirely. Repair is significantly cheaper than replacement and is a viable option.

items.title: Oil consumption
items.whatHappens: Like many high‑revving performance engines, the S65 can develop increased oil consumption as it ages. Consumption of up to 1 litre per 1,000 km is not uncommon on higher‑mileage units.
items.repairVsReplace: Regular oil level monitoring and top‑ups are the standard approach. If consumption becomes excessive, valve stem seals or piston rings may need attention - this typically requires a rebuild.

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the S65B40
variants.intro: The S65B40 is a specific engine code within the S65 family, not a code that fragments into multiple UK‑market sub‑codes. The S65 family includes: - S65B40 - 4.0L, 414 hp, fitted to standard E90/E92/E93 M3 (UK market) - S65B44 - 4.4L, 444 hp, fitted to limited‑production M3 GTS and M3 CRT (not UK‑market regular production) The S65B40 is sometimes referred to as S65B40A in BMW parts systems. How to confirm your code: 1. On the engine - the S65B40 code is stamped on the engine block. Look for "S65B40A" on the identification plate on the left‑hand side of the engine. 2. On the V5C logbook - the engine number is listed; cross‑reference with BMW parts systems. 3. VIN decode - use a BMW VIN decoder; E9X M3 vehicles will show engine type "S65B40A". 4. Registration lookup - enter your reg above and we'll confirm the exact fitment. Similar‑looking codes it is commonly confused with: - BMW S55B30 - the turbocharged straight‑six successor in the F80 M3; not related and not a swap - BMW S54B32 - the straight‑six predecessor in the E46 M3

relatives.description: - the legendary straight‑six from the E46 M3, producing 338 hp from 3.2 litres. The S65B40 replaced it with a V8 configuration, adding 76 hp and a higher 8,300 rpm redline, but also introduced the rod‑bearing issues that the S54 largely avoided.

- the twin‑turbo straight‑six that replaced the S65 in the F80 M3 and F82 M4. It produces 425-450 hp with significantly more torque than the S65, but purists regard the naturally aspirated S65 as the last great high‑revving M engine.

variants.closing: Why fitting the wrong revision matters: The S65B40 is unique to the E9X M3. The S65B44 (4.4L) from the GTS is not a direct fit for standard M3s without significant modification, and the S55 is a completely different engine family (turbo straight‑six) requiring full drivetrain and electrical changes.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement S65B40 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used S65B40 makes sense only if the donor engine has documented proof of recent rod bearing replacement (within the last 20,000 miles) and full service history with 10W‑60 oil. The primary risk with used units is undisclosed bearing wear - insist on an oil analysis and bore scope before purchase. For lower‑value E9X M3 examples, a used unit with proven bearings can be a cost‑effective option. View used engines

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper S65B40 recon includes new rod bearings (upgraded clearance bearings from ACL or BE Bearings), new throttle actuators, new VANOS components, fresh gaskets and seals, and a full machining check of the crankshaft and block. This is the right call for most replacements - you get a like‑new unit with the known weak points already addressed, backed by 12-24 months warranty. View reconditioned engines

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified for high‑value, low‑mileage or collectable E9X M3s where originality matters. An upgraded rebuild should include BE or ACL rod bearings with increased clearance, ARP main studs, and a full crankshaft polish or replacement if scored. For standard applications, reconditioned is usually more cost‑effective. View rebuilt engines

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: All engines can be supplied and fitted through our network of vetted UK BMW M specialists - nationwide coverage with 12‑month warranty on labour and parts. View supply & fit
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: The S65B40 sits exclusively in E9X M3s, which currently range from £10,000-£35,000 depending on condition, mileage and specification (saloon, coupé, convertible). A £6,500-£9,500 reconditioned engine plus £1,000-£1,500 fitting is a significant investment - typically 30-60% of the vehicle's value. For lower‑value examples (sub‑£12,000), carefully evaluate the car's overall condition, bodywork and interior before committing to a replacement. For collectable low‑mileage or special‑edition cars, the investment is usually justified.

items.question: What are the common problems with the BMW S65B40 engine?
items.answer: The S65B40's most critical weakness is rod bearing wear due to tight factory clearances, typically appearing at 60,000-80,000 miles. Other issues include throttle actuator failure (gears wear out) and increased oil consumption at higher mileage. Rod bearing failure can write off the entire engine. Preventative bearing replacement costs £1,500-£2,500. Throttle actuator rebuild is cheaper than replacement.

items.answer: The S65B40 is stamped on the engine block (left-hand side) with "S65B40A" on the identification plate. You can also decode your VIN - E9X M3s show engine type "S65B40A". items.question: Is the S65B40 reliable if I replace the rod bearings?
items.answer: Yes - with the rod bearings addressed preventatively, the S65B40 is a robust and durable engine. Many owners report 100,000+ miles without major issues beyond routine maintenance. The throttle actuators are also fixable, and oil consumption is manageable with regular top-ups. Preventative bearings are the single most important upgrade. Use BE or ACL bearings with increased clearance. Regular oil changes with 10W-60 are essential.
